### Gentrification
Gentrification accelerated significantly after 2000, though it remains geographically concentrated [ev-1]. Since 2000 nearly **20** percent of lower-income neighborhoods experienced gentrification, more than double the rate of the **1990s**, which saw only **9** percent [ev-1]. Nationally, only **8** percent of all neighborhoods reviewed since the **2000** Census have gentrified [ev-1]. The phenomenon is defined by increases in median home values and educational attainment among residents who were previously in the bottom **40th percentile** for income and housing value within their metro area [ev-1].

The most intensive gentrification occurred in select cities. Portland led with **58.1%** of eligible tracts gentrifying (**36** gentrified vs. **26** that did not out of **142** total) [ev-1]. Washington D.C. followed at **51.9%** (**54** gentrified, **50** not, **75** ineligible, **179** total), Minneapolis at **50.6%** (**39**, **38**, **39**, **116**), and Seattle at **50%** (**7**, **7**, **118**, **132**) [ev-1]. In terms of raw numbers, New York had the highest count with **128** gentrified tracts out of a total of **2,152** (with **301** not gentrifying and **1,723** ineligible) [ev-1]. Other cities with high rates included Atlanta (**46.2%**), Virginia Beach (**46.2%**), Denver (**42.1%**), Austin (**39.7%**), Sacramento (**30%**), Oakland (**29.3%**), Philadelphia (**28.7%**), Albuquerque (**28.1%**), San Diego (**27.5%**), Baltimore (**23.2%**), Long Beach (**22.4%**), Fort Worth (**21.5%**), Omaha (**21.4%**), Nashville (**21.1%**), Boston (**21.1%**), and San Francisco (**18.8%**) [ev-1]. Cities like Detroit (**2.8%**), Las Vegas (**2%**), El Paso (**0%**), and Arlington, TX (**0%**) experienced little to no gentrification [ev-1].

Demographically, gentrifying neighborhoods saw their non-Hispanic white population share increase by an average of **4.3** percentage points and poverty rates drop by **0.7** percentage points [ev-1]. In contrast, eligible tracts that did *not* gentrify saw a **5.0**-point decline in the white population share (a relative decrease as minorities increased) and a **6.7**-point rise in poverty [ev-1]. Gentrifying tracts also recorded a total population change of **+6.5%** compared to a **-2.4%** loss in non-gentrifying eligible tracts [ev-1].

### Income Inequality
Income inequality has widened across major U.S. cities since 1980, with urban cores exhibiting higher disparities than suburbs or rural areas [ev-11]. The national Gini coefficient reached record levels, rising from **0.40** in **2013** to **0.485** in **2018**, **0.488** in **2020**, and **0.494** in **2021** [ev-3][ev-11]. Metropolitan areas often show even steeper increases; for instance, New York City had a Gini index of **0.5469** [ev-2][ev-11], while Atlanta (**0.57**) and Miami (**0.57**) were also high, with New Orleans at **0.56** [ev-11].

Using the 95/20 income ratio (comparing top earners to those at the 20th percentile), the national average rose from **8.5** in **2007** to **9.3** in **2014**, with large cities averaging an even higher ratio of **11.8** compared to metro areas' **9.7** [ev-5]. In **2014**, **57** of the **100** largest metropolitan areas had significantly higher inequality ratios than they did in **2007** [ev-5][ev-11].

City-specific data highlights extreme disparities:
*   New Orleans has the highest income inequality among major U.S. cities, with a ratio of **7.87**: the 80th percentile earns **$110,820** while the 20th percentile earns only **$14,078** [ev-4].
*   Boston follows closely at **7.81**, with the 80th percent earning **$172,476** and the 20th percent earning **$22,095** [ev-4].
*   Newark ranks third with a ratio of **6.80** (**$161,577** vs. **$23,758**) [ev-4].
*   Jersey City is fourth at **6.09** times more earnings for the upper quintile than the lower [ev-4][ev-1].
*   New York City ranks sixth at roughly **5.8** times greater earnings for top earners compared to low-income counterparts [ev-4].

In some metros like Atlanta and Washington D.C., the 95/20 ratio reached as high as **18:1**, meaning the 95th percentile earns **18** times more than the 20th [ev-11]. Incomes near the bottom dropped substantially between **2007** and **2014**; in fact, double-digit slides in 20th-percentile incomes were common across large metro areas during this period [ev-5].

### Affordability
The gap between income growth and housing costs has widened for decades. Since **2000**, median household income grew by only **92%** (from **$41,990** to **$80,610**), while median home prices nearly tripled, jumping **177%** from **$122,775** to **$339,937** [ev-6]. On an inflation-adjusted basis, household incomes increased just **8.5%**, whereas home prices rose more than **56%** [ev-6]. By July **2024**, the Case-Shiller Index reached **325.78**, representing a **225%** increase since January **2000** [ev-11].

Affordability crises are most severe in California and other major hubs. Five of the six large U.S. cities with the highest price-to-income ratios are in California: Los Angeles (**9.6**), San Jose (**12.2**), Long Beach, San Francisco, and San Diego all top the list with ratios ranging from **9.6** to **12.2** [ev-6][ev-11]. These figures are more than double the national average ratio of roughly **4.6–4.7** [ev-6][ev-8]. Other major cities facing similar pressures include New York City, Miami, and Boston [ev-6]. In contrast, Chesapeake, VA has one of the most equal income distributions among large cities, where high earners make only **3.8** times as much as low earners, with a minimum threshold for high earners of **$152,000** [ev-4].

### Displacement
Displacement from gentrification is not uniform; it disproportionately affects minority communities due to racially stratified housing markets and discriminatory lending practices [ev-9]. A study in Philadelphia found that financially disadvantaged residents moving from historically Black gentrifying neighborhoods tended to move to poorer non-gentrifying neighborhoods within the city, facing fewer affordable options than their white counterparts who moved from other gentrifying areas into wealthier suburbs or cities [ev-9][ev-11]. This occurs because there are "fewer affordable neighborhoods" overall as cities transform, shrinking residential options for disadvantaged minorities while expanding them for advantaged groups [ev-9].

The economic shift driving these changes includes a decline in manufacturing jobs (from **19.5** million in **1979** to under **11.5** million during the pandemic) and a surge in finance and professional services employment (from **12** million to **32** million), which concentrated high-income professionals in large urban cores like Washington D.C. and San Francisco since **1980** [ev-8][ev-11]. Consequently, nearly **80** percent of the country’s growth in its population under age **45** has been concentrated in metro areas with over one million residents since **1980**, while rural and small metro counties have seen declines or stagnation in this demographic [ev-8]. Urban populations also became more educated and diverse; by recent counts, **35%** of urban residents hold a bachelor's degree or higher (compared to **31%** in suburbs and **19%** in rural areas), and whites are now a minority in most urban counties (**53%**) compared to only **10%** of suburban counties being majority nonwhite [ev-7][ev-11].
